visible.summary:
Podlaskie saw Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event: at the 20 July 2019 Białystok Equality March, roughly 1,000 marchers were attacked by thousands of far-right and football-hooligan groups who attempted to block the route. Police detained 25 people; 32 counter-demonstrations had been registered that day, including a prayer vigil at the Cathedral Basilica. In the run-up, Archbishop Tadeusz Wojda had a proclamation read in every church across the region. The surrounding Białystok County had been declared an LGBT-free zone in 2019, though the city itself did not adopt one, and its mayor questioned whether the march was "needed" while the PiS city council filed a motion to stop it.

The state's protective response improved materially: at the fourth Equality March (28 September 2024), ~300 participants were escorted by 500 police officers and the Podlaskie police reported zero incidents. This is positive evidence under the single-incident rule (institutional learning, proportionate deployment), but it does not erase the 2019 pattern—organised mass violence met with a partial 25-person detention response, embedded in a documented church-and-county mobilisation infrastructure.

Score of 0.44 sits 0.08 below the national 0.52. Slightly above Subcarpathian (0.42), which lacked Podlaskie's demonstrable five-year improvement in state protection, but below Masovian (0.56), where the institutional machinery runs the other way.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2019 mass assault and the 2024 well-policed march concerned equality-march participants - LGBT people broadly, including trans participants - rather than a trans-specific instrument; the region's hostility-and-protection trajectory is a general public-presence signal that colours how a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor reads local safety.

sources.claim: Reference article on the Białystok Equality March: the first march took place 20 July 2019 with approximately 1,000 participants and was attacked while far-right groups attempted to block the route; the surrounding Białystok County had been declared an 'LGBT-free zone' in 2019, and Podlaskie's voivodeship was a PiS stronghold. Anchors the record's claim of Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event with dates and scale.

Local Podlaskie outlet report (28 September 2024): the IV Equality March in Białystok drew about 300 participants guarded by around 500 police officers (spokesman Tomasz Krupa); counter-demonstrations appeared at several points along the route, but the regional police stated after the gathering that no incidents were recorded and assessed the event as safe. Dated 2024 update: continued far-right presence but peaceful outcome under heavy police cover.

visible.summary:
Lubelskie carried a voivodeship-level "LGBT-free" resolution from 2020 until its 20 September 2021 repeal under European Commission funding pressure. Its municipality of Świdnik (population ~40,000) was the first local authority in all of Poland to adopt an anti-LGBT resolution (March 2019, "against homopropaganda, LGBT ideology and the early sexualisation of Polish children"), and its deputy council chair explained the act explicitly as opposition to Warsaw's LGBT+ Declaration signed a month earlier. Świdnik became the template copied by roughly 100 authorities nationwide.

The resolution is now formally gone, but as with other eastern voivodeships the repeal was coerced rather than converted—the underlying civic mobilisation that produced Poland's first-ever anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto signal. No march violence or ban is documented at the voivodeship scale beyond the general resolution-era hostility.

Score of 0.45 sits 0.07 below the national 0.52. Above Subcarpathian (0.42), which additionally produced a mayoral march ban and held out until 2025, and above Podlaskie (0.44), where the 2019 coordinated mass assault adds a violence dimension absent in Lublin. Below Małopolska (0.48), which pairs its resolution history with Kraków's clearly positive institutional trajectory.
visible.tangentialFactors: The resolution history targeted 'LGBT ideology' broadly rather than trans status specifically; with the document repealed, no formal instrument remains, but the mobilisation that produced Poland's first anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto general-hostility signal.

sources.claim: ZOiS Spotlight 14/2020 (8 April 2020): Świdnik — a town in south-east Poland, in the Lublin voivodeship — became the country's first 'LGBT-free zone' when its county council passed a non-binding resolution in March 2019 pledging to protect children from 'homosexual propaganda' and to refrain from actions encouraging 'tolerance of LGBT people'. Scholarly framing of the record's Świdnik-first claim, plus the resolution's embedding in global anti-gender campaigning.

The Them (23 September 2021, updated 29 September): on Monday 20 September 2021 the provinces of Podkarpackie, Małopolska and Lubelskie repealed their 'LGBT-free' resolutions — Lubelskie notable because it had previously voted to keep it, and all repeals following European Commission funding threats. Confirms the record's voivodeship repeal date of 20 September 2021 under EU pressure.

visible.summary:
Małopolska adopted a voivodeship-level "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution in 2020, repealed on 20 September 2021 under EU funding pressure, placing it in the same five-region configuration as the eastern belt. The regional declaration carried the same intent as its siblings: to exclude a visible public LGBTQ presence from the voivodeship's civic space.

Within the same unit, however, Kraków—the capital and Poland's second city—has moved decisively the other direction. In May 2024 newly elected mayor Aleksander Miszalski announced he would become the first Kraków mayor ever to attend the city's LGBT Equality March and would fly a rainbow flag at city hall. His predecessor Jacek Majchrowski (2002–2024) had only become an honorary patron of the march in 2021 and never attended. For a visitor in Kraków's old town, the operative institutional signal is the mayor's public presence, not the repealed voivodeship document.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52: the resolution history pulls it down, Kraków's positive trajectory prevents a deeper drop. Above Lublin (0.45), where no equivalent capital-city counter-signal exists, and well above Subcarpathian (0.42), where the capital actively banned a march. Below Masovian (0.56), where Warsaw's institutional machinery works continuously in the visitor's favour.
visible.tangentialFactors: Both poles - the repealed voivodeship resolution and the capital mayor's march attendance - concern LGBT public presence broadly rather than trans status specifically; they set the general institutional climate a trans visitor reads locally, without trans-specific enforcement either way.

sources.claim: The Them (23 September 2021, updated 29 September): Małopolska's voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on Monday 20 September 2021 alongside Podkarpackie and Lubelskie, after European Commission funding threats — Małopolska notable because council leader Jan Duda (father of president Andrzej Duda) had only weeks earlier voted to keep the zone. Confirms the record's 2020-21 voivodeship arc and its EU-pressure repeal date.

Notes from Poland (9 May 2024): newly elected Kraków mayor Aleksander Miszalski announced in one of his first decisions that he would attend the city's annual LGBT Equality March — becoming the first Kraków mayor to do so, after a predecessor who declined — and pledged to hang a rainbow flag at city hall, writing that he wants 'a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone'. Dated local-government signal of warming climate in the voivodeship's capital.

visible.summary:
Łódzkie was one of the five voivodeships that formally adopted an "anti-LGBT ideology" resolution by mid-2020, placing approximately one-third of Poland's territory under declarations whose stated purpose was to exclude LGBTQ public events. It sits in the PiS-vote heartland belt running east of the Łódź metro area. The resolution was struck down or repealed in the 2021 wave following EU Commission funding threats.

No march ban, coordinated attack, or county-level holdout comparable to Subcarpathian's Łańcut (2025) or Podlaskie's Białystok County is documented for Łódzkie. The sub-national finding is the regional resolution itself and its location in the eastern conservative bloc; the practical visitor-facing exposure is the general social climate of that bloc rather than a specific enforcement or violence event.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52, matching Małopolska (0.48) for having a voivodeship-level resolution without an additional capital-city positive counterweight or a documented enforcement/violence episode. Well above Subcarpathian (0.42) and Podlaskie (0.44), both of which carry specific ban or assault evidence.
visible.tangentialFactors: The voivodeship resolution was an anti-LGBT-ideology declaration (LGBT broadly, not trans-specific) and is formally gone; the visitor-facing residue is the eastern bloc's general civic climate rather than any enforcement or violence event documented for this unit.

sources.claim: Per-voivodeship revocation record: the Supreme Administrative Court of Poland revoked Łódź Voivodeship's anti-LGBT resolution on 12 October 2023, and the Świętokrzyskie voivodeship council revoked its own resolution on 22 September 2021 (the European Commission had written to the governors of five voivodeships — Lublin, Łódź, Lesser Poland, Podkarpackie, and Świętokrzyskie — on 2 June 2020 about the resolutions). By 24 April 2025 all anti-LGBTQ resolutions and all Local Government Family Rights Charters in Poland had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order.

Between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 Polish local governments adopted ‘LGBT-free zone’-style resolutions which at their peak covered roughly a third of the country's land area; Polish administrative courts struck them down as unconstitutional (Article 32 equal treatment), the European Commission linked EU development funds to their repeal, and the last remaining zone (in Łańcut) was abolished in 2025. The article notes the resolutions were symbolic and institutional rather than criminal — they created no new penalties and barred no one physically — but signalled to local bureaucracies and schools which families and identities local leadership considered legitimate.

Located in the same eastern conservative bloc as Łódzkie and Lubelskie, its resolution was annulled or repealed in the 2020–2021 court-and-EU-pressure wave.

No march ban, violence episode, or holdout municipality comparable to the Subcarpathian or Podlaskie findings is documented at the voivodeship scale. The visitor-facing signal is the regional declaration's intent to exclude LGBTQ public presence and the social climate of the PiS heartland belt; the formal legal document is now absent.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52, identical to Łódzkie (0.48) on shared evidence: both are resolution-carrying voivodeships in the eastern bloc without unit-specific enforcement or violence findings beyond the declaration itself. Above Lublin (0.45), which additionally contains Świdnik, Poland's first-ever anti-LGBT municipal resolution.
visible.tangentialFactors: The regional resolution targeted 'LGBT ideology' broadly rather than trans people as such; with the document gone, what remains visitor-facing is the declaration-era civic climate of the ruling party's heartland belt, not any unit-specific instrument.

visible.summary:
Masovian, anchored by Warsaw, is the institutional counterweight to Poland's eastern resolution belt. On 6 February 2024, Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last remaining "against LGBT ideology" document in the country. Warsaw is the origin point of the progressive response: in February 2019 Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed a 12-point LGBT+ Declaration (security, education, culture, sport, employment; drawn up with LGBT NGOs, including an intervention hostel and school "lighthouse keeper" projects), which provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution (Świdnik, March 2019) as an explicit counter-reaction. The administrative-court campaign, led from Warsaw by the national Commissioner for Human Rights and carried through the provincial administrative courts and the Supreme Administrative Court, dismantled the resolution network nationally.

The unit's dark stain is historical: in May 2005 the city under mayor Lech Kaczyński banned that year's Parada Równości, and the ECtHR in Bączkowski and Others v. Poland (2007) ruled the ban violated Articles 11, 13, and 14 ECHR. This is 20 years past and has not been repeated; the current institutional trajectory is clearly positive.

Score of 0.56 sits 0.04 above the national 0.52. The only unit scoring above national in this dossier; well above Małopolska (0.48) and the eastern belt (0.42–0.45), where the resolution legacy dominates and no equivalent court-repeal or declaration infrastructure exists.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2019-2025 resolution fight and the EU funding conditionality concerned LGBT+ rights broadly (family-charters and sex-curriculum language rather than gender-expression enforcement) - their force for trans visitors is the institutional signal they carried.
visible.localsOnly: The Warsaw declaration's operational measures - the intervention hostel for rejected teenagers and the school support projects - serve residents; a visitor uses none of them but reads the institutional climate they created.

sources.claim: Wikipedia's consolidated 'LGBT-free zone' overview records the full arc: by January 2020 a third of Poland's territory had passed anti-LGBT resolutions; on 6 February 2024 Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last document 'against LGBT ideology' in Poland; by 24 April 2025 every anti-LGBTQ resolution and Family Charter endorsement was withdrawn or court-invalidated.

URBACT's March 2019 account of Warsaw's LGBT+ Declaration: Mayor Trzaskowski signed the capital's pledge of equality, non-discrimination and hate-crime response, and the piece documents the declaration's politics and reception in Warsaw — the 2019 commitment freshness confirms shows no record of repeal.
